scenes.tts: In a resting neuron, potassium leaks out and sodium leaks in, all the time. So why does the voltage hold still?
scenes.visual: A neuron outline on a dark background. Purple K+ dots stream out through the membrane and orange Na+ dots stream in, continuously. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: In a resting neuron, potassium leaks out and sodium leaks in, all the time. So why does the voltage hold still?

scenes.tts: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at about minus seventy-one millivolts.
scenes.caption: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at about −71 mV.
scenes.visual: A voltmeter beside the cell reads −71 mV. Small label: made-up cell; numbers invented.
scenes.narration: Here is a made-up neuron, resting at about −71 mV.

scenes.tts: Potassium current leaves it all the time, about two hundred picoamperes. Sodium current comes in, about the same amount.
scenes.caption: Potassium current leaves it all the time, about 200 pA. Sodium current comes in, about the same amount.
scenes.visual: Two arrows on the membrane: a purple outward arrow labelled K+ about +200 pA, an orange inward arrow labelled Na+ about −200 pA. The dots keep streaming.
scenes.narration: Potassium current leaves it all the time, about 200 pA. Sodium current comes in, about the same amount.

scenes.tts: Neither ion is at equilibrium. Yet the voltmeter needle does not move.
scenes.visual: The dots keep streaming while the voltmeter needle stays fixed at −71 mV. The needle is highlighted.
scenes.narration: Neither ion is at equilibrium. Yet the voltmeter needle does not move.

scenes.tts: Start with one term. Each ion has an equilibrium potential.
scenes.visual: The cell shrinks to a corner. A title card: equilibrium potential, E_ion.
scenes.narration: Start with one term. Each ion has an equilibrium potential.

scenes.tts: It is the voltage where the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient. There, the ion has no net push.
scenes.visual: Definition card: E_ion = the voltage where electrical force balances the concentration gradient; no net push in or out. Two opposing arrows of equal size appear under it.
scenes.narration: It is the voltage where the electrical force on the ion balances its concentration gradient. There, the ion has no net push.

scenes.tts: Now picture a voltage scale. Potassium's equilibrium potential sits near the left end, at minus ninety-five millivolts.
scenes.caption: Now picture a voltage scale. Potassium's equilibrium potential sits near the left end, at −95 mV.
scenes.visual: A horizontal voltage scale draws across the screen. A purple mark near the left end: E_K = −95 mV.
scenes.narration: Now picture a voltage scale. Potassium's equilibrium potential sits near the left end, at −95 mV.

scenes.tts: Sodium's sits near the right end, at about plus sixty millivolts.
scenes.caption: Sodium's sits near the right end, at about +60 mV.
scenes.visual: An orange mark near the right end: E_Na = +60.6 mV. A tick marks 0 mV.
scenes.narration: Sodium's sits near the right end, at about +60 mV.

scenes.tts: A marker on the scale shows the membrane potential, the inside minus the outside.
scenes.visual: A teal marker labelled Vm appears at −71.2 mV. Small label: Vm = inside − outside.
scenes.narration: A marker on the scale shows the membrane potential, the inside minus the outside.

scenes.tts: The gap between the marker and an ion's own mark is the driving force. Its sign gives the direction of the current. Its size gives the strength.
scenes.visual: A bracket spans from the purple mark to the marker, labelled driving force = Vm − E_K. A second bracket spans from the marker to the orange mark, labelled Vm − E_Na.
scenes.narration: The gap between the marker and an ion's own mark is the driving force. Its sign gives the direction of the current. Its size gives the strength.

scenes.tts: Tie a rope from the marker to each ion's mark. The rope's pull is that ion's current.
scenes.visual: A purple rope runs from the marker to E_K, an orange rope to E_Na. Label: pull = current.
scenes.narration: Tie a rope from the marker to each ion's mark. The rope's pull is that ion's current.

scenes.tts: More open channels make a thicker rope. That is conductance, how open the ion's path is.
scenes.visual: The purple rope thickens; label: rope thickness = conductance, g (nS).
scenes.narration: More open channels make a thicker rope. That is conductance, how open the ion's path is.

scenes.tts: And a rope pulls harder the farther the marker sits from its mark.
scenes.visual: A ghost marker slides away from E_K and the purple rope glows brighter as it stretches, then returns. Label: longer stretch = bigger driving force.
scenes.narration: And a rope pulls harder the farther the marker sits from its mark.

scenes.tts: So current equals conductance times driving force.
scenes.caption: So current equals conductance times driving force: I = g × (Vm − E).
scenes.visual: On screen, held: I_ion = g_ion × (Vm − E_ion). The bracket (Vm − E_ion) is labelled driving force.
scenes.narration: So current equals conductance times driving force: I = g × (Vm − E).

scenes.tts: By convention, outward current, positive charge leaving, counts as positive.
scenes.visual: A small card beside the equation: outward current (positive charge leaving) = positive; inward = negative.
scenes.narration: By convention, outward current, positive charge leaving, counts as positive.

scenes.tts: Our cell rests above potassium's mark. Which way does potassium flow through its open channels?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. Vm = −71.2 mV, E_K = −95 mV. Which way does K+ current flow?
scenes.narration: Our cell rests above potassium's mark. Which way does potassium flow through its open channels?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Outward. The driving force on potassium is positive, so positive charge leaves.
scenes.visual: On screen only: Vm − E_K = −71.2 − (−95) = +23.8 mV. A purple arrow points out of the cell, labelled outward.
scenes.narration: Outward. The driving force on potassium is positive, so positive charge leaves.

scenes.tts: Sodium is the opposite. The marker sits far below sodium's mark, so sodium is pushed in, hard.
scenes.visual: On screen only: Vm − E_Na = −71.2 − 60.6 = −131.8 mV. A long orange inward arrow.
scenes.narration: Sodium is the opposite. The marker sits far below sodium's mark, so sodium is pushed in, hard.

scenes.tts: Potassium has much more conductance, but a short stretch. Sodium has less conductance, but a long stretch.
scenes.visual: The purple rope is thick and short; the orange rope is thin and long. On screen only: g_K = 8.47 nS, g_Na = 1.53 nS.
scenes.narration: Potassium has much more conductance, but a short stretch. Sodium has less conductance, but a long stretch.

scenes.tts: The two currents come out equal and opposite, about two hundred picoamperes each way.
scenes.caption: The two currents come out equal and opposite, about 200 pA each way.
scenes.visual: On screen only: I_K = 8.47 nS × 23.8 mV = +202 pA; I_Na = 1.53 nS × (−131.8 mV) = −202 pA. The two arrows are drawn the same width.
scenes.narration: The two currents come out equal and opposite, about 200 pA each way.

scenes.tts: That is what rest means. Zero net current, not zero current for each ion.
scenes.visual: Card: rest = zero NET current. The dots keep streaming both ways while the needle stays still.
scenes.narration: That is what rest means. Zero net current, not zero current for each ion.

scenes.tts: Two puzzles remain. Why does the cell rest here, and not somewhere else?
scenes.visual: Puzzle 1 appears on screen: Where does it rest, and why there? The marker on the scale pulses.
scenes.narration: Two puzzles remain. Why does the cell rest here, and not somewhere else?

scenes.tts: And what if we push a little current in? How big a change, how fast, and how far does it reach?
scenes.visual: Puzzle 2 appears below: What does a small nudge do? How big, how fast, how far?
scenes.narration: And what if we push a little current in? How big a change, how fast, and how far does it reach?

scenes.tts: One rule answers both. Each ion's open channels pull the voltage toward that ion's equilibrium potential.
scenes.visual: Both ropes tug the marker toward their own marks. Banner: each ion's open channels pull Vm toward that ion's E.
scenes.narration: One rule answers both. Each ion's open channels pull the voltage toward that ion's equilibrium potential.

scenes.tts: Rest means the currents cancel, not that they stop.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: rest = the currents cancel, not stop.
scenes.narration: Rest means the currents cancel, not that they stop.
